TUT1_3: And this is the enemy Hero - me! You win battles by killing all the opposing enemy Heroes.
TUT1_4: And if your Hero dies, well... I'm sure you can figure out what that means.
TUT1_5: Tap on your Hero now to select him.
TUT1_6: Your Hero can move and attack once per turn. Move him forward by tapping the circle with the arrow inside.
TUT1_7: He is now in range of the enemy Hero. Select your Hero and then Tap on the enemy to attack.
TUT1_8: Ouch! You may have noticed the little numbers under the Heroes.
TUT1_9: The Red symbol is Power - this is how much damage your attacks deal.
TUT1_10: The Green symbol is Health. You may have noticed I started with 6, and now have 5.
TUT1_11: This is a turn-based game, so let's end the turn to progress.
TUT1_12: Destroying the enemy Hero wins the game. Come get me!
TUT1_13: Well, that hurt! Hey, have you noticed the big number? It's your Mojo.
TUT1_14: Your Hero generates Mojo each turn, which is used to play cards and use special abilities.
TUT1_15: Here's a little gift, a Monster Card!
TUT1_16: You will notice this card costs 3 Mojo to cast. (The purple number in the top/left corner of the card).
TUT1_17: Tap down and drag the card toward your Hero. This will cost 3 Mojo, as displayed on the card.
TUT1_18: Monsters can only be summoned near your Hero.
TUT1_19: Freshly summoned Monsters are Exhausted. They can attack but not move. End the turn to continue.
TUT1_20: This Monster is a Warrior. Warriors are generally tough, but only have a range of 1.
TUT1_21: Warriors can also choose to move a second time instead of attacking. Neat!
TUT1_22: Have a go at attacking me with your new forces.
TUT1_23: Here, let me give you a new toy.
TUT1_24: Take this new Equipment Card. It's a Dagger; Warriors can use these.
TUT1_25: Conveniently your Hero is also a Warrior. It's like I thought this through!
TUT1_26: Drag the dagger onto one of your creatures to give it to them.
TUT1_27: Warriors can use all melee weapons. Archers use Bows, and Mages use Staves.
TUT1_28:
Use your new bling to defeat the Enemy Hero. Yeah, I used a colloquialism. I'm cool like that.

// Tutorial 2
TUT2_1: You did so well in the last Tutorial that I gave you a new card. Isn't it pretty?
TUT2_2: There are hundreds of cards in this game, so you'll have to choose wisely when building your deck.
TUT2_3: But I'm getting ahead of myself. Check out your new card; a Mage!
TUT2_4: Mages can attack enemies that are two tiles away. Summon this Mage to continue.
TUT2_5: End the turn so we can replenish our Mojo. Trust me, we're going to need it!
TUT2_6: Some Monsters have special Abilities. Select your Mage to see his Ability.
TUT2_7: This mage has Fireball. It costs 2 Mojo to cast, but is quite powerful. Select it now.
TUT2_8: To fire it, you must be in range. Give it a go and then end the turn.
TUT2_9: Hah! Eat that. Not so smart now, are you?
TUT2_10: I guess this is a bit one-sided. Here, have an Archer.
TUT2_11: Archers are sneaky. They can attack enemies that are three tiles away!
TUT2_12: On the downside, they can't hit things that are right in front of them.
TUT2_13:
Now try to defeat me!

// Tutorial 3
TUT3_1: Are you ready for a proper fight?
TUT3_2: Check out this new card. Runes have passive effects and must be placed on Rune stands.
TUT3_3: You only have a limited number of Rune stands based on the map you're playing, so choose wisely.
TUT3_4: Select your new Rune to continue.
TUT3_5: This Rune grants you additional Mojo each turn. Drag it onto a Rune Stand to activate it.
TUT3_6: Now you will generate extra Mojo each turn. Check it out by ending the turn.
TUT3_7: See? Now you're getting 5 Mojo each turn. That's very useful.
TUT3_8: Did you notice this card? It's a spell. Select it now.
TUT3_9: This Spell gives you Mojo for each Rune you own. Drag it anywhere onto the field to activate it.
TUT3_10: Of course that spell costs 3 to cast and you only had one Rune, so it's more effective if you have more Runes.
TUT3_11: Levels will often have bonus tiles on the ground. Let's put a Monster on this Defence Tile.
TUT3_12: The Monster now has 2 Defence, but only while it's standing on the bonus tile.
TUT3_13: Defence is like Health but it replenishes every turn like Mojo, making it very useful.
TUT3_14: You can also use Equipment cards like Shields to gain Defence. There are even some Runes that can do it.
TUT3_15: This is a Power Tile. Anything that stands on it gets +2 Power.
TUT3_16: And this is a super-important Mojo tile. You earn +2 Mojo each turn for each Mojo tile you're standing on.
TUT3_17: That's it. You're ready for the big leagues now! Defeat me to complete this tutorial.

HELP_LB_1:
As you will see when you enter the online lobby, all players have an associated star rating next to their names.

This rating is based on their overall performance as tracked using the Elo ratings system.

A nine star player is the best of the best, with lower numbers indicating lesser success rates.
HELP_LB_2:
When you finish an online game, a certain amount of points are added to, or subtracted from, your running total.

WINNING:
There is a subtlety here in that winning the battle isn't strictly the definition of when you score - you actually get points for killing a player's hero*.

This distinction means that you can still earn some points for a kill in a 6P game, even if you don't eventually go on to win the entire battle. It's done this way to ensure that multiplayer games do not become an inefficent way to make progress up the leaderboard.

How many points you actually score is based on whose hero you just killed and what type of battle you're in, explained below.

(* If a player disconnects at the end, you still get the win and points for being 'last man standing'.)

LOSING:
When (and if) your hero dies, you will lose points equivalent to your own star rating. If you are a four star player, you will lose four points.

Because people have a natural aversion to negative numbers, the leaderboard starts each month with everyone on 1,000 points.
HELP_LB_3:
When you kill someone's hero, the points you score for the leaderboard depends on that player's star rating, possibly modified based on the type of battle being played.

Async Battle:
Star rating x LBMUL_ASYNC.

Realtime Ruck:
Star rating x LBMUL_RT.

Clash of the Clans:
Star rating x LBMUL_CLAN.

In any sort of team battle, when a player kills a hero, ALL players on that team get the points.
HELP_LB_4:
At the end of each month, prizes are awarded to the top 100 players and then the whole thing resets.

"Affliction" is a catch-all term for any lasting effects an attack might leave on a creature. They will either last one round or forever, and fall into one of two categories - good and bad.

Some spells and abilities might act to remove a particular affliction, whilst others might act on good or bad ones collectively.

Remember that any creature stepping on to a regen tile will have all bad afflictions cured instantly.

HELP_GAMEPLAY_1:
Each player has to bring a hero into combat, the objective being to control the last one alive.

When your hero dies, that's game over for you, so try to keep it safe.

You can attack enemies with your hero, but the safer option is to spawn monsters and let them do your fighting.
HELP_GAMEPLAY_2:
Monsters will form the backbone of your strategy to winning in combat - the clue is in the game title!

You can deploy monsters into combat during your own turn, but keep in mind that it's your hero who calls them forth, which means monsters can only be spawned on an empty space adjacent to your hero.

Use your spawned monsters to attack your enemies, but try to remember that whilst killing the enemy's hordes can be fun, you only have to kill their hero to win the battle.
HELP_GAMEPLAY_3:
Prior to starting a battle, you need to make a "deck". All of the various monsters and other items exist in card form, and it is your job to mix these cards together into a coherent deck.

This deck is shuffled at the start of combat and you then draw an initial "hand" of six cards. You also draw one card at the start of each of your turns*.

On your own turn, you can then play these cards onto the battlefield to spawn monsters etc.

(* Because going first can otherwise give a slight advantage, the starting player does not draw an additional card on their first turn.)
HELP_GAMEPLAY_4: Every card has a Mojo cost required to play it. If you don't have enough Mojo at the time, you will not be able to do so. This cost can be seen as a purple number at the top/left of all card imagery.\n\nYou can earn Mojo in various ways, but your Hero conveniently generates Mojo for you at the start of your turn - exactly how much depends upon the Hero you pick.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_1:
Monsters are the bread and butter of the game, and we recommend you fill at least a third of your deck with them.

Each monster card spawns a real life monster onto the battlefield, but that monster's various powers and abilities all come from what's written on the card.

Tap and hold on any battlefield monster during combat and you will be shown a large view of the monster card plus any extra cards for equipped items, etc.

Below is a description of everything you will see on the large card view for a monster, and how it relates to gameplay.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_2: This is how much power your monster starts off with. When it performs any kind of attack, it is this value that is used to determine the amount of damage dealt to the victim.\n\nThere are many in-combat modifiers for a monster's power at any one moment, but the card view will always show just the starting value.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_3:
This is how much health (or life) your monster starts off with.

When attacked, the attacker's power is subtracted from the victim's health. When a monster's health drops to zero, well - you can figure out what happens to it next!

There are many in-combat modifiers for a monster's health at any one moment, but the card view will always show just the starting value.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_4:
All cards, not just monsters, have a rarity icon. This does not directly affect any in-combat statistics, but is an indicator of how regularly a given card will show up in a booster chest.

It stands to reason though that the rarer the card, the generally better it will be.

HELP_MONSTERCARDS_5: All cards have a Mojo cost required to play them. You earn this Mojo in many different ways, the most direct of which being your hero, who generates some at the start of each of your turns.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_6: There are many different races of monster in the game. Each monster belonging to a particular race will receive that race's bonus in combat, all the time, as a passive ability.\n\nThese racial bonuses are specifically designed to encourage certain deck-building strategies, but working with different races in the same deck can develop a near infinite number of fun combinations of deck synergy.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_7: A lot of monsters, but not all, come with their own specialised skill beyond a basic attack. If they have one, it will be described on the card.\n\nDuring combat you may select these additional abilities instead of performing a basic attack, provided you have the Mojo to pay for it.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_8:
A monster's name should be obvious enough, but its class merits further explanation.

There are four different classes of monster within each race, Warriors, Archers, Mages and Artillery. Each of these classes have signature abilities, for example Warriors tend to have more Power and Health, whereas Archers are generally weaker but can fire further.

The most important thing to note though, is that you have to match the various weapons cards to their owner's class. You cannot put a bow on a Mage, nor can you put a Mages Staff on a Warrior. Etc.

Weapons and their use is described in more detail under the "Other Cards" topic.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_9:
Warrior class creatures have an attack range of 1.
This means that they must be directly adjacent to the target to perform a basic attack or use an activated ability on it.

As an added bonus, warrior monsters can take an additional move at the expense of not attacking on that turn.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_10: Mage class creatures have an attack range of 1 - 2.\n\nThis means they can attack or use their ability on any valid target that is either adjacent or one space away from them.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_11: Archer class creatures have an attack range of 2 - 3.\n\nThis means they can attack or use their ability on any valid target that is two or three spaces away. Note that they cannot fire at "point blank" range.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_12: Artillery class creatures have an attack range of 3.\n\nThis means they can attack any valid target that is exactly three spaces away. Note that they cannot both attack and move on the same turn.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_13: Some activated abilities don't use a creature for a target, but select a map space for some sort of area effect.\n\nIn these cases you will be shown the valid locations you can pick, and the card will describe the range and effect of the ability.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_1:
Apart from the obvious Monsters, there are several different core types of cards you might want to put in your deck.

Each of these types bring different benefits, and a well constructed deck will usually feature at least a few cards from each.

Because screen space is limited, cards come in two sizes. Most of the time you will see an abbreviated smaller version, but if you tap and hold on one, a larger view will be presented.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_2:
As there are four different classes of monster - Warriors, Archers, Mages and Artillery - there are also four classes of weapon to go with them.

You will note that the different classess of monster cards have uniquely coloured backgrounds, and these are repeated on the their matching weapons cards.

Mages may only be equipped with Staffs, Archers may only be equipped with Bows, whilst Warriors can use all the rest, referred to as "Melee Weapons"

Every weapon has a Power "buff", noted in the top/right corner, that adds to its bearer's Power for as long as the weapon is in hand.

Some weapons may do other things as well, such as causing an Affliction on the defender.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_3:
Armour cards can be played onto your own spawned monsters that are already on the battlefield.

Like most cards, armour can bring other benefits as well, but the main thing they do is give your monster some defence.

Defence (Shields and Armour) works similarly to health in that it absorbs damage. When an attack comes in, damage is dealt to the defence first, and only if there is any surplus does the remainder get applied to the defending monster's health.

For example, if a monster with 2 Health and 2 Defence is attacked by a monster with 3 Power, the first 2 Power goes into the defence and the remaining 1 Power then gets taken off the defender's health. It just escaped with it's life!

Once a shield has absorbed it's fill in damage, it no longer functions until the start of your next turn, at which time it is fully recharged.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_4: Shields function in the same way as armour and are collectively referred to as "defence". Graphically, a shield will appear on an equipped monster's arm, whereas armour appears as a helmet, chest plate and shoulder pads ensemble.\n\nBecause defence is always a good thing, you are allowed to equip a monster with both a shield and some armour should you wish.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_5:
Spells all have some sort of instant effect on the battle.

These effects vary a lot, such as dealing damage to monsters, drawing extra cards, getting more mojo, etc.

You will have to read each card to see what's available, but a well timed spell can turn a battle.

To cast a global spell, simply drag the card from your hand anywhere onto the battlefield. For targetted spells, drag over a valid target, which will light up in the usual way, and let go whilst over it.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_6:
Runes are the "permanently on" version of spells, and generally provide for similar types of effects.

For example a spell to draw two cards will work just the once, whereas a rune to draw a card will draw a card at the start of each of your turns, indefinitely - full details will be written on the card.

Because runes are more powerful than spells, you are limited to how many you can have in play at once.

To play a rune you must drop it onto the Rune Stand of your own colour, of which there are typically two to four in total, based on the battlefield layout.

(In skirmish or online games, there are always exactly four.)

You can play a new rune over an old one to replace it. (Doing so does not count as destroying it.)

Like monsters, runes have health (they all start at RUNICSTARTHEALTH) and can be attacked by creatures. Once a rune's health is reduced to zero, it is destroyed and disappears. Note that to attack a rune, the attacking monster must be stood adjacent to the rune regardless of its class.

The casting cost for a rune is face value mojo plus 2 more for each similar rune already in play under your control.
HELP_BOOSTERS_1: Rubicoins are the game currency in Combat Monsters. You earn these coins in various ways through continued gameplay, and can then spend them on booster chests or purchasing single cards from the collection view.
HELP_BOOSTERS_2:
You get free coins from the following game activities:

1) Beating quests.
Each battle of each quest has a prize for winning - Rubicoins and sometimes booster chests too. The amount of Rubicoins you earn is based on the quest difficulty and your current level.
These prizes can only be claimed once per battle, and later on per deck rules type.

2) Completing a Skirmish Battle.
You get some coins each and every time you win a Skirmish Battle. Again your level will also provide additional income here.

3) Winning in online battles.
You earn Rubicoins for being the last person standing in an online battle. Private battles are just for fun though.

4) Achievements.
Each achievement you unlock will also provide a one time coin boost. You can see your achievements progress by tapping the large button at top/right of the main menu.
HELP_BOOSTERS_3:
You can also purchase Rubicoins for real money via the Store page.


Because we value your custom, we have several offers available with growing discounts to match increased outlay. You can purchase these offers as often as you like in any combination. The amount of coins you get depends on how much you spend and how many times you've levelled up in the game. Play makes it cheaper.
HELP_BOOSTERS_4: As you level up through winning battles, your Loyalty Bonus will also increase.\n\nThis bonus, used as percentage, is applied to the base amount of coins available for purchasing through the store page, so the more you play, the more coins you can buy for the same amount of money.
HELP_BOOSTERS_5:
There is one other thing you can buy for real money, and that is the Rubicoin Tripler.

As the name might indicate, once you've purchased this awesome accelerator, all Rubicoins you earn through the above-mentioned gameplay events will be tripled forever.

This is the best and cheapest single thing you can do to swell your card collection rapidly.
HELP_BOOSTERS_6: The main things you will want to spend your hard-earned coins on are booster chests.\n\nBooster chests come in several flavours, at different coin prices, and contain 6 or 12 new cards, selected at random, to swell your card collection and help improve your decks.
HELP_DECKEDITOR_1:
There is always an active deck. If you are new to the game, this will be the one you picked for free at the start.

Whenever you pick a deck, to start a Skirmish Battle for example, this becomes the active one.

When you open the deck editor it will be this deck loaded, and when you tap save, your edits will be saved back over this deck.

To make a copy of a deck, use the "Save As" button. From their you can pick one of many slots to save into, but whichever one it is, this becomes the new active deck.
HELP_DECKEDITOR_2:
The bottom row of cards in the editor view is actually your deck. As long as you save it with between 30 and 200 cards, you will be able to pick it in future to enter a battle.

To remove cards from your deck, simply drag them toward the other row of cards at the top of the display.

To add cards to your deck, drag them down onto your card list from that top row.
HELP_DECKEDITOR_3: The row of cards along the top is only a subsection of your full card collection, filtered by something. The buttons just below this row change the filter between monsters, weapons, spells, etc.\n\nSlide the controls up and down to alter the filter settings and refine the upper card pool to your liking.

HELP_QUICKBATTLE_1: When you've had your fill of beating the quests, we recommend starting to play online against other real people, as this is where Combat Monsters truly shines. Not only can it be great fun, but you will see lots of new deck ideas and playing strategies to help improve your own game.\n\nHowever, we accept that online play is not for everyone, so for them we present the Skirmish Battle option.
HELP_QUICKBATTLE_2:
Skirmish Battle is meant to be a real challenge and victory won't come easily here, even for seasoned players. You can try to win a Skirmish Battle with a starter deck, but good luck with that!

The enemy computer players get the following advantages over you, based on the difficulty setting chosen:

1) They start with some extra cards.

2) They get some extra mojo each turn.

3) Their decks are awesome.
HELP_QUICKBATTLE_3:
1) Random Enemy Deck:
Before play, the computer selects a random deck from its large and nasty library, and matches that with the best hero to play it with.

2) Random Layout:
The layout is also chosen at random from those available for online battles.

3) Rubicoins:
You earn coins for winning, should you ever manage that.

4) Good luck!
You're gonna need it...
HELP_MULTI_1: Pass and Play is a gameplay mode that allows two players to play on one machine. The decks and heroes come from the host's collection, and the guest player must also use these.\n\nPlay alternates in the usual way, but it's up to the players to play in turn. Only two players are supported.
HELP_MULTI_2:
You may also play Combat Monsters online against other people from around the world. Play is cross-platform, so all players will find each other regardless of what device they are playing on.

Before play starts you pick your deck, hero and the number of players in the game from 2 to 6. The game then starts automatically once all players are present.

Rubicoins are available for winning, and you get leaderboard points for killing enemy heroes. How many depends on their star rating, which is a loose indicator of their ability and experience.
HELP_MULTI_3: Regardless of which type of multiplayer game you start/join, the layouts (or "maps") are always randomised from a large selection, appropriate to the number of players.\n\nSimilarly, who plays first and the order of play is also completely randomised each time a game starts.
HELP_CLANS_1:
Tap the Clan Room button on the main menu. From there you will be able to create a new clan just by giving it a name. You will automatically become the leader and can then go on to recruit other members. There is a search option to find players by name and you can tap their names to send an invite. Players already in a clan will not be shown though.

If someone else has already invited you to their clan, you will see a message in the Clan Room to that effect.

Clan membership has three levels. The creator of the clan is the 'Leader' and can recruit new players, kick existing players, edit the clan flag and/or promote other members to 'Scout'.
Scouts can recruit other members without further permission from the leader. Everyone else is a basic 'Member'.
HELP_CLANS_2:
If you want to play in a team battle (i.e. 2v2) with your clanmates, just start one and players will automatically be seated together according to their clan membership.

A 'normal' team battle though might have random opponents playing as the other team, it's first come first served.

If you specifically want to play one clan vs another, select the 'clans' version of the team battle options instead - i.e. 'Clans 2v2'. As the lobby fills up, players will not be allowed to join if they're either not in a clan or their clan membership would exceed the number of teams allotted.
HELP_CLANS_3:
The Clan Room has a special leaderboard that ranks each clan in a similar way to the online players one.

If you are a member of a clan, any points you win or lose from online battles will also affect your clan's running total - this applies for all game types including 1v1 realtime and async, regardless of whether your opponent is in a clan or not.

The small ones with numbers in show a player's ability level. We keep track of who beats who to show a rough indication of player skill. People with higher star ratings are demonstrably better players, although rookies are provisionally given 3 stars as a starting point.

When you beat someone, their star rating becomes the points you get for doing so, and these are what are totalled to sort the leaderboard. If you lose, you drop your own star rating in points.

The large star without a number shows that the player placed on the leaderboard last month.
